title: Freelance Difficult Client Kit
description: Handle difficult clients calmly, and end the relationship cleanly when you need to. A 16-point red flags scorecard for before and during the work, a fill-in working-hours policy with a completed example, 12 ready-to-send scripts for late feedback, scope creep, ghosting, overdue invoices and rude messages, an exit guide with three routes and a 15-step checklist, seven exit emails, and an incident log with a worked example.

files.README.md:
# Freelance Difficult Client Kit

Most difficult client relationships don't start difficult. They drift: a late-night message you answer once, a payment that's a week late, a "quick call" that becomes daily. This kit helps you spot the drift early, respond calmly in writing, and, when it can't be fixed, end the relationship cleanly without burning your reputation.

It's for any freelancer who works directly with clients: designers, developers, writers, marketers, consultants, virtual assistants, photographers.

## The system in one paragraph

Before you sign, score the client against **red flags** and protect yourself in the terms. When you start, send a short **working-hours policy** so expectations are written down. When something goes wrong, **log it** the same day and reply with a calm **script** that names the issue and the next step. If the same issue comes back three times, or one serious line is crossed, use the **exit guide** to decide how to end it, and the **exit emails** to do it.

## What's inside

| File | What it's for |
|---|---|
| `red-flags-scorecard.md` | 16 warning signs to check before you sign and during the work, with a scoring guide |
| `working-hours-policy.md` | Fill-in communication policy (response times, channels, urgent requests), with a completed example |
| `difficult-situations-scripts.md` | 12 calm, ready-to-send replies for the situations freelancers ask about most |
| `ending-a-client.md` | When to end it, three exit routes (after the project, at a milestone, immediately), and a 15-step exit checklist |
| `exit-emails.md` | Seven emails for ending a client relationship politely and clearly |
| `incident-log.csv` | A simple record of what happened and when, with a worked example |

## Start here

1. **Today:** fill in `working-hours-policy.md` and save it as a template. Send it to your next new client at kickoff.
2. **For any client who already feels difficult:** start an `incident-log.csv` entry for every issue from now on, and run them through the "during the work" part of `red-flags-scorecard.md`.
3. **Next time something happens:** find the matching script in `difficult-situations-scripts.md`, adjust it, and send it the same day. Don't wait until you're angry.

## Three rules that make everything else work

1. **Write it down.** Agreements made on calls get forgotten or remembered differently. After every call where something is decided, send a two-line email: "To confirm what we agreed: ...".
2. **Respond to the issue, not the tone.** You can't control how a client writes. You can control whether your reply is calm, specific and ends with a clear next step.
3. **Decide before you're desperate.** It's much easier to step back from a client when you have other work coming in. Keep looking for new clients even when you're busy.

## A note on contracts and the law

This kit gives general information and templates, not legal advice. What you can do when a client won't pay, or when you end a contract early, depends on what your contract says and the law where you and the client are. If a dispute involves a large amount, or a client threatens legal action, talk to a lawyer or a local small-business advice service before you reply.

## If a client is abusive

Rudeness and pressure are things this kit helps you handle. Threats, harassment, or discrimination are different. You don't have to manage those with a polite script. Stop work, keep a copy of every message, end the relationship in writing (email 7 in `exit-emails.md`), and get advice if you feel unsafe or the client threatens you.

# Scripts for 12 Difficult Situations

Each script follows the same pattern: **acknowledge**, **state the fact or the agreement**, **give the next step**. Keep replies short. Send them during your working hours, and never while you're angry: write it, wait an hour, then read it again before sending.

Replace everything in [brackets].

---

## 1. Messages outside your hours, expecting a fast reply

> Hi [name], thanks for this. I'm picking it up now that I'm back [this morning]. [Answer or next step.] Just a reminder that my working hours are [hours], so anything sent outside them will get a reply the next working day. If something's urgent, [the urgent route] is the best way to reach me.

## 2. Feedback is late but the deadline hasn't moved

> Hi [name], thanks for the feedback. Because it arrived [four] days after the date in our schedule, the next delivery moves from [old date] to [new date]. If [old date] is important, let me know: I may be able to keep it as a rush job at [rush price], or we could reduce what's in this round.

## 3. A new request presented as part of the original scope

> Hi [name], good idea. Looking back at our agreement, [the thing] wasn't part of the original scope, which covered [what was agreed]. I'm happy to add it: it would be [price] and move delivery to [date]. Shall I go ahead?

## 4. Approved work is reopened

> Hi [name], I can certainly look at [the homepage] again. We signed it off on [date] ([attached / see email]), so changes now count as new work. The cost would be [price], and it would affect [anything that depends on it]. Would you like me to go ahead, or keep the approved version?

## 5. The client goes silent mid-project

Send the first message, then the second a week later if there's no reply.

> Hi [name], just checking in on [the item you're waiting for]. I'm ready to carry on as soon as I have it. Is [date] realistic?

> Hi [name], I haven't heard back about [the item], so I've paused work on [project] for now. When you're ready, let me know and I'll fit it into my next available slot, which is currently [date]. As agreed, I'll invoice for the work completed so far at the end of this month.

## 6. Invoice is overdue and reminders have been ignored

> Hi [name], invoice [number] for [amount] was due on [date] and is now [number] days overdue. I've sent reminders on [dates]. Please could you let me know today when it will be paid? Until it's settled, I'm pausing work on [project], in line with the payment terms in our agreement.

Only pause work if your agreement allows it, and say so plainly. If it doesn't, change your terms for the next project.

## 7. A rude or blaming message

> Hi [name], thanks for letting me know you're unhappy with [specific thing]. I want to get this right. Could you tell me which parts aren't working, and what you'd like to see instead? Once I have that, I'll come back with a plan by [date].

Respond only to the specific complaint. Don't match the tone, don't defend yourself at length, and don't apologise for things that weren't your fault. If the message is abusive rather than rude, see the end of `README.md`.

## 8. "Can you just do this quickly, it'll only take five minutes?"

> Hi [name], happy to help. Even small changes need a bit of time to set up, check and send back, so my minimum for extra tasks is [minimum fee / 30 minutes at my hourly rate]. If that works, I'll do it by [date].

## 9. Too many people giving feedback

> Hi [name], I've had feedback from [three] people on this round, and some of it pulls in different directions (for example, [A] wants [X] and [B] wants [Y]). To keep us on schedule, could you combine everything into one list and decide on the points that conflict? Then I'll get straight on it.

## 10. A decision made on a call is later denied

> Hi [name], I understand how this can get confusing. On our call on [date], we agreed [decision], and I confirmed it by email afterwards ([attached]). I've built the work on that basis. If you'd now like to go a different way, I can quote for the change. Let me know which you'd prefer.

This only works if you sent the summary. Start doing it after every call.

## 11. A request to lower the price after the work is done

> Hi [name], I understand budgets can change. The price was agreed on [date] for [scope], and the work has been delivered as agreed, so the invoice stands at [amount]. If there's a specific part you're unhappy with, tell me and I'll look at it. If the budget for future work is smaller, let's talk about scope before the next project.

## 12. Let's reset how we work

Use this when several small issues add up and you want to fix the relationship rather than end it.

> Hi [name], I've enjoyed working on [project] and want to keep doing great work for you. Lately a few things have made it harder for me to deliver at my best: [two or three specific, neutral examples, such as "feedback has been arriving after the deadline" or "requests are coming through several channels"].
>
> To keep things running smoothly, from [date] I'll [the change: e.g. "move delivery dates when feedback is late", "take requests by email only", "quote new items before starting"]. I've attached my working-hours note as a reminder of how I work.
>
> I think this will make things easier on both sides. Happy to talk it through if helpful.

---

## What not to send

- Long explanations of how hard you've been working
- Anything sarcastic, or with "as I said before" or "per my last email"
- Threats you won't follow through on
- Replies in the middle of the night

# Ending a Client Relationship

Ending a client is a business decision, not a failure. Done well, it protects your time and income, and the client usually leaves with a reasonable impression of you.

## Is it time? Five questions

Answer yes or no.

1. Has the same issue come back three or more times, even after you named it and used a script?
2. Is the client's "during the work" red flag score 8 or more, or rising each month?
3. Is your effective hourly rate on this client well below your average (money received ÷ all hours, including messages and calls)?
4. Is this client stopping you from taking on better work, or affecting your other clients?
5. Has the client crossed a line you won't accept (abuse, discrimination, asking for something dishonest or illegal, refusing to pay for delivered work)?

**Any yes to question 5:** end it now. Use the immediate exit route.
**Three or more yeses to 1 to 4:** plan your exit. Pick a route below.
**One or two yeses:** try a reset first (script 12 in `difficult-situations-scripts.md`) and look again in a month.

## Before you decide: the money check

- What share of your income comes from this client?
- How many months of essential costs could you cover if it stopped?
- Is other work in your pipeline?

If losing the client would leave you short, you can still decide to leave, but time the exit: finish the current project, line up replacement work, then step back.

## Three exit routes

| Route | When to use it | What it looks like |
|---|---|---|
| **After the project** | The relationship is tiring but working; you just don't want more | Finish everything as agreed, deliver, invoice, then decline new work |
| **At a milestone** | The project is long or ongoing, and continuing will cost more than stopping | Give notice, finish the current stage, hand over, invoice for completed work |
| **Immediately** | A serious line is crossed, or the client has stopped paying | Stop work, send written notice, invoice for completed work, hand over what's been paid for |

**Check your contract first.** Look for a termination clause (how much notice either side must give), what happens to payment for work in progress, and who owns unfinished work. If your contract says nothing, give reasonable notice anyway (two to four weeks is common for ongoing work) and be clear about what you'll bill. If a lot of money is involved or the client disputes it, get advice before you send anything.

## The 15-step exit checklist

**Prepare**

- [ ] 1. Re-read your contract: notice period, payment terms, ownership of work
- [ ] 2. List all work completed, in progress and not started
- [ ] 3. Work out the final invoice: completed work, plus in-progress work at an agreed or fair proportion, minus any deposit already paid
- [ ] 4. Collect everything the client will need: files, passwords you hold for them, documents, notes
- [ ] 5. Choose your exit date and the email you'll use from `exit-emails.md`

**Tell them**

- [ ] 6. Send the exit email during working hours, early in the week
- [ ] 7. If they ask for a call, agree, but confirm everything by email afterwards
- [ ] 8. Don't negotiate on the decision itself. You can be flexible on timing and handover.

**Hand over**

- [ ] 9. Deliver all paid-for files in an organised folder with a short guide to what's where
- [ ] 10. Return access: change or hand over any passwords, remove yourself from their accounts, confirm in writing
- [ ] 11. Send the final invoice with the handover
- [ ] 12. Offer one or two referrals if you know someone suitable, and only if you'd be comfortable recommending the client to them

**Close**

- [ ] 13. Record the exit in `incident-log.csv` with the date and final status
- [ ] 14. Keep the contract, invoices and key emails for as long as your local rules on business records require
- [ ] 15. Write down one lesson for your next contract or kickoff (for example, "add a feedback deadline clause")

## What to say if they push back

- **"Can't you just finish it?"** "I understand this isn't ideal timing. I'll make sure everything up to [stage] is complete and handed over properly, so whoever continues can pick it up easily."
- **"We'll give you more money."** "Thank you, I appreciate that. My decision isn't about the rate, so I'll stick with the plan, but I'm glad to help with a smooth handover."
- **"You can't do this."** "Our agreement allows either of us to end it with [notice period]. I've given that notice and I'll complete everything due before [date]." (If your agreement doesn't say this, offer reasonable notice and get advice if they threaten action.)
- **"Why?"** Give one short, neutral reason or none. "It's no longer the right fit for how I work." You don't owe a list of their faults.
files.exit-emails.md:
# Seven Exit Emails

Replace everything in [brackets]. Keep them short and neutral. Send during working hours, and keep a copy of everything you send.

---

## 1. Declining before you start

> Subject: Your [project]
>
> Hi [name],
>
> Thank you for thinking of me for [project]. Having looked at the brief and timeline, I don't think I'm the right fit for this one, so I'll step aside rather than take it on and not give it the attention it needs.
>
> [Optional: You might find [type of specialist / a named colleague] a better match.]
>
> Best of luck with it.
> [your name]

## 2. Declining further work after a project

> Subject: Thank you, and my availability
>
> Hi [name],
>
> Thanks for the work on [project]. Everything is now delivered: [summary of what's delivered and where].
>
> Looking ahead, I'm focusing on [type of work / a smaller number of clients], so I won't be able to take on further projects for you. If it helps, [name or type of freelancer] could be a good fit for future work.
>
> All the best,
> [your name]

## 3. Ending an ongoing arrangement with notice

> Subject: Notice: [retainer / ongoing work]
>
> Hi [name],
>
> I'm writing to give notice that I'll be ending our [monthly retainer / ongoing arrangement]. In line with our agreement, my last working day on your account will be [date], [notice period] from today.
>
> Until then, everything continues as usual. Before [date], I'll:
> - finish [current items]
> - send all files and documents in [an organised shared folder]
> - hand over or remove any access I have to your accounts
>
> My final invoice will cover [period] and be sent on [date].
>
> Thank you for the work together. I'll make sure the handover is smooth.
> [your name]

## 4. Stopping at a milestone in a project

> Subject: [Project]: next steps after [milestone]
>
> Hi [name],
>
> I've decided that after completing [milestone, e.g. the design stage] I won't continue to [the next stage]. I'll deliver [what's included at the milestone] by [date], with everything organised so another [designer / developer / writer] can pick it up easily.
>
> My final invoice will be for [the milestone amount / the work completed to date], less the deposit of [amount], making [total]. Work on [next stage] hasn't started, so there's nothing further to bill.
>
> I'm sorry for any inconvenience. I'm happy to answer questions from whoever takes it on for [two weeks] after handover.
> [your name]

## 5. Pausing for non-payment

> Subject: Work paused: invoice [number]
>
> Hi [name],
>
> Invoice [number] for [amount] is now [number] days overdue, despite reminders on [dates]. As set out in our agreement, I've paused all work on [project] from today.
>
> Work will restart within [two] working days of payment. If I haven't received payment or heard from you by [date, about two weeks away], I'll treat the project as ended, send a final invoice for all completed work, and look at the options for recovering what's owed.
>
> If there's a problem with the invoice, please tell me and we'll sort it out.
> [your name]

## 6. Ending after non-payment

> Subject: Project ended: [project]
>
> Hi [name],
>
> Following my email of [date], I haven't received payment for invoice [number] or a reply. I'm therefore ending my work on [project] from today.
>
> The total now outstanding is [amount] ([invoice numbers]). Please pay by [date]. Once payment is received, I'll send [the final files / the completed work] as agreed.
>
> [your name]

Before sending, check what your contract says about ownership of work that hasn't been paid for, and get advice if a large amount is involved.

## 7. Ending immediately (serious lines crossed)

> Subject: Ending our work together
>
> Hi [name],
>
> I'm ending my work on [project] with immediate effect, because [brief, factual reason: e.g. "of the messages received on [date]"].
>
> My final invoice for the work completed to date, [amount], is attached. Once it's paid, I'll send [the files for the completed work].
>
> I won't be continuing the conversation by phone or messages. Anything further should be sent to this email address.
> [your name]

Keep this one short. Don't argue the reason, and don't respond to further messages except about payment and handover.

files.red-flags-scorecard.md:
# Red Flags Scorecard

Use the first section before you agree to any project, and the second at any point during the work. Score each flag 0 (not present), 1 (a little) or 2 (clearly present). Most clients score a few points; that's normal. What matters is the total and whether it's rising.

## Before you sign

| # | Red flag | What it often means | Score |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | They want to start before agreeing on price or scope | Scope and price will keep moving later | |
| 2 | They push hard on price before understanding what you'd do | Price will be the only thing they value | |
| 3 | "It's a quick job" or "should be easy" before you've seen the brief | They don't know how much work it is, and won't pay for the real amount | |
| 4 | They ask for free samples or a test project unpaid | They may collect free work from several freelancers | |
| 5 | Unclear who decides ("I'll need to check with a few people") | Feedback from many directions and slow approvals | |
| 6 | They criticise every previous freelancer | You may be the next one on the list | |
| 7 | Very tight deadline that they caused | Their urgency becomes your emergency, repeatedly | |
| 8 | They resist a deposit or a written agreement | Payment problems are likely | |
| | **Total before signing** | | **/16** |

**0 to 4:** go ahead with your normal terms.
**5 to 8:** go ahead only with protection: a deposit of at least 50%, a fixed scope, a set number of revision rounds, and a named decision maker.
**9 or more:** politely decline, or quote a price that genuinely covers the extra risk and time. Email 1 in `exit-emails.md` is a polite decline.

## During the work

| # | Red flag | Score |
|---|---|---|
| 9 | Messages outside agreed hours, expecting a fast reply | |
| 10 | Feedback arrives late but deadlines stay the same | |
| 11 | New requests presented as part of the original scope | |
| 12 | Approved work is reopened ("actually, can we go back to...") | |
| 13 | Invoices paid late, or only after reminders | |
| 14 | Calls or messages that are rude, dismissive or blaming | |
| 15 | Decisions agreed in calls are later denied | |
| 16 | You feel anxious opening their messages | |
| | **Total during the work** | **/16** |

**0 to 3:** normal friction. Handle each issue with a script and move on.
**4 to 7:** reset expectations. Send the working-hours policy again (or for the first time) and use script 12 ("Let's reset how we work") in `difficult-situations-scripts.md`. Start logging every issue.
**8 or more, or rising each month:** start planning your exit. See `ending-a-client.md`.

Flag 16 counts. Your own stress is information, not weakness. Ask yourself whether the client's behaviour or your own setup (no policy, no written scope) is causing it, and fix whichever you can.

## Worked example

Jo, a freelance copywriter, scored a new client at 3 before signing (a tight deadline and "should be quick"). Jo took a 50% deposit and wrote a fixed scope. Six weeks in, the "during" score was 7: weekend messages (2), late feedback with fixed deadlines (2), two reopened approvals (2), and some anxiety (1). Jo sent the working-hours policy and a reset email. A month later, the score was 3. The client stayed, and paid on time from then on.
files.working-hours-policy.md:
# Working Hours and Communication Policy

Send this at the start of every project, as part of your kickoff email or welcome document. It's not a contract, just a clear, friendly description of how you work. Clients are usually glad to know.

Replace everything in [brackets]. A completed example is at the bottom.

---

## How I work

**My working hours** are [Monday to Friday, 9:00 to 17:30], [time zone]. I don't check messages outside these hours, so anything sent in the evening or at the weekend will be answered on the next working day.

**Reply times.** I reply to emails within [one working day]. If something needs more thought, I'll tell you when you can expect a full answer.

**Where to reach me.** Please send project messages by [email to address / in our shared project channel]. Messages sent elsewhere (personal phone, social media) might be missed. I keep everything in one place so nothing gets lost.

**Calls.** Calls are best booked ahead using [my booking link / by email]. I keep [Tuesday and Thursday afternoons] for calls, so my other days can be spent on the work itself. After each call I'll send a short summary of what we agreed.

**Feedback.** Please send feedback as one combined list per round, from [one person], by the date in our schedule. If feedback arrives late, the next delivery date moves by the same number of days.

**Urgent requests.** If something is truly urgent (for example, [the website is down or there's an error in something already published]), [email with URGENT in the subject / text me on number]. I'll do my best to respond the same day. New work requested with less than [three working days'] notice is charged at [1.5 times] the normal rate, and I'll always confirm the price before starting.

**Time off.** I'll let you know about any holidays at least [two weeks] in advance, with a plan for anything due around that time.

---

## Completed example

> Hi Marta,
>
> Really looking forward to this project. A few quick notes on how I work, so you always know what to expect:
>
> - **Hours:** Monday to Thursday, 9:00 to 17:00 (London time). I don't work Fridays or weekends, so anything sent then gets a reply on Monday.
> - **Replies:** within one working day by email.
> - **Where:** please send everything to this email address. It's the one place I check for project messages.
> - **Calls:** book any time on Tuesday or Wednesday afternoons using the link in my signature. I'll send a summary after each one.
> - **Feedback:** one combined list per round from you, by the date in the schedule. If feedback comes in late, the next delivery moves by the same number of days.
> - **Urgent:** if something already published has an error, put URGENT in the subject line and I'll reply the same day. New work with less than three working days' notice is charged at 1.5 times my normal rate, always confirmed with you first.
>
> Any questions, just ask. First drafts are due on 14 March.
>
> Priya

---

## Making it stick

- **Follow your own policy from day one.** If you answer a Saturday message within ten minutes once, the client learns that's normal.
- **Schedule, don't send.** If you work late, write replies but schedule them to send during your working hours.
- **Turn off notifications** for client channels outside your hours.
- **Point back kindly.** If a client breaks the policy, reply in your hours and reference it lightly: "Thanks for this, picking it up now that I'm back in on Monday."
